title: esp32c3: calling ticks_us() repeatedly hangs when IRQ is disabled
body: I am using an ESP32-C3 with MicroPython up to commit f1bdac375240941edfc0aa04b646dc3c53d6b371. If I disable IRQ, wait for about 1000us using a ticks_us() busy loop, and then restore the IRQ state, the board hits an interrupt watchdog timeout and restarts. The same loop runs when I remove the disable_irq() and enable_irq() calls. I expect the program to run in both cases.

symptoms_visible: On my ESP32-C3, a roughly 1000us ticks_us() busy loop runs normally with interrupts enabled, but with interrupts disabled the board reports an interrupt watchdog timeout and restarts.
N0.label: N0 ESP32-C3 watchdog reset reported

symptoms_visible: My complete function already saves the state returned by machine.disable_irq() and passes it to machine.enable_irq(); it still ends in a watchdog reset.
N1_x.label: N1_x IRQ-state usage correction

symptoms_visible: The full g_dbg1 function prints 'start', disables interrupts, enters the ticks_us() loop, and resets before printing 'stop'; g_dbg2 without IRQ masking always completes.
Even a requested interval of 1ms triggers the reset although the configured interrupt-watchdog timeout is 300ms.
N1.label: N1 complete reproducer established

symptoms_visible: With interrupts disabled, three reduced tests—collecting ticks_us() values, building a list of integers, or just running an empty for loop—hang at about 32 iterations.
If I disable the interrupt watchdog, the reduced test hangs forever instead of resetting.
N2.label: N2 operation threshold and blocked stack collected

symptoms_visible: The test does not crash immediately before commit 337742f6c70a7b9d407df687774bb9c9cc6a1656 and does crash immediately after it.
The same failure is seen on ESP32-C6, while tests on ordinary ESP32 and ESP32-S2 boards complete.
My ESP32-C3 reproduces the hang with ESP-IDF 5.0.4, 5.0.7, and 5.2.2.
N3.label: N3 regression and platform scope established

symptoms_visible: With my locally patched firmware, the IRQ-disabled timing loop completes correctly instead of hanging.
N4.label: N4 reporter workaround installed

symptoms_visible: My locally patched ESP32-C3 firmware completes the IRQ-disabled loop, but I did not report retesting an upstream build containing the accepted fix.
N_terminal.label: terminal upstream fix accepted without reporter retest

solution.intent: Treat the reset as misuse of the IRQ API and restore the exact state returned by machine.disable_irq().
solution.concrete_example: Save state = machine.disable_irq(), then call machine.enable_irq(state) rather than enabling interrupts without the saved state.

edges.comment: Opening exchange c0-c1 on the reporter's ESP32-C3: participant1 assumed the saved IRQ state was omitted, but the reporter supplied the complete function showing that it was already passed to enable_irq and the watchdog reset remained.

question_patterns: Are you passing the value returned by machine.disable_irq() back to machine.enable_irq()?
Can you confirm how you restore the previous interrupt state?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes. I save it as st_irq = machine.disable_irq() and later call machine.enable_irq(st_irq).

counterfactual_candidates.answer: No, I was calling machine.enable_irq() without the saved state; passing it back makes the reset disappear.

question_patterns: Can you provide the complete minimal functions for the failing and working cases?
Please show the exact reproducer, including the calls around the timing loop.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: My failing g_dbg1 prints 'start', saves st_irq from machine.disable_irq(), waits with tm_til = ticks_us() + 1000 and while ticks_us() < tm_til: pass, restores st_irq, and prints 'stop'. The matching g_dbg2 omits only the disable and enable calls and always completes.

edges.comment: Reporter c1 describes the reporter's own ESP32-C3 and corrects the initially abbreviated reproduction. The 1ms-versus-300ms observation and pulse-timing use case were volunteered in the same reply.

question_patterns: Can you paste the complete failing and working functions?
What exact code still resets after restoring the saved IRQ state?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The complete g_dbg1 saves and restores st_irq around a 1000us ticks_us() busy loop, but it resets before printing 'stop'. g_dbg2 contains the same loop without masking interrupts and always prints 'stop'.

edges.comment: Recovery from the rejected c0 suggestion using the reporter's clarification in c1. The target retains the already-established fact that the returned state was restored.

question_patterns: Can you reduce the loop further and determine whether the failure depends on elapsed time or the number of operations?
What happens if, after disabling IRQ, the code only runs a simple list comprehension or empty loop?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I reduced it to three versions: collecting ticks_us(), collecting i, and just 'for i in range(n): pass'. All three behave the same and hang when n reaches about 32 while IRQ is disabled.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: A simple empty loop can run indefinitely; only ticks_us() calls cause the hang.
The threshold is 31 or 33 iterations depending on the exact bytecode, but the time spent in the loop does not determine it.

question_patterns: If you disable the interrupt watchdog, does the program continue or remain stuck?
Can you test whether the watchdog is the cause or only detects the hang?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: When I disable CONFIG_ESP_INT_WDT, it hangs forever instead of rebooting.

question_patterns: Can you attach a debugger when it hangs and paste the top frames of the backtrace?
Where is execution blocked once the watchdog is disabled?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The stopped backtrace begins in vPortYield(), called from mp_thread_mutex_unlock(), and then mp_execute_bytecode().

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The debugger is blocked inside the hardware timer read used by ticks_us(), with no vPortYield or mutex-unlock frame.

edges.comment: Reporter c5 supplied the reduced bytecode loops and watchdog-disabled result. Participant2 c6 supplied the debugger stack from an affected setup; the affected contributors are folded into one simulated user side. The raw stack is retained without putting the deadlock conclusion in the user's answer.

question_patterns: Can you test revisions around the point where this started and identify the first bad commit?
Does a checkout immediately before and after the suspected change reproduce differently?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes. I tested immediately before and after 337742f6c70a7b9d407df687774bb9c9cc6a1656: before it the code does not crash, and after it the code crashes.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The reproducer already fails before that commit, and there is no behavior change across it.
The same first bad commit is found using a wider pair of good and bad revisions.

question_patterns: Can this be reproduced on other ESP32 variants, particularly another RISC-V board and an Xtensa single-core board?
Which other ESP32-family targets pass or fail the reduced test?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The C6 shows the same problem. A genuine ESP32 and an ESP32-S2 complete the test without this hang.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: It fails identically on ESP32-S2 and ordinary Xtensa ESP32 boards as well as the C3.

question_patterns: Does changing the ESP-IDF version alter the failure on the same ESP32-C3?
Which ESP-IDF versions have you tested with this reproducer?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I tested ESP-IDF 5.2.2, 5.0.4, and 5.0.7 on my C3, and the problem remains.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: It only fails with ESP-IDF 5.0.4; rebuilding the same MicroPython revision with 5.2.2 fixes it.

edges.comment: Reporter c9-c11 provided the raw before/after revision result. Participant1 c13 and c23 supplied C6 and S2 results, while the reporter c25 supplied the ESP-IDF version tests. These affected setups are explicitly folded into the simulated user side; identifying the FreeRTOS contract violation remains engineer inference.

solution.intent: Use the reporter's temporary workaround: suppress the forced context switch while interrupts are disabled.
solution.concrete_example: Before requesting the forced context switch, check whether IRQ is currently disabled and skip the switch in that state.

edges.comment: Reporter c14 installed a local patch that checks the IRQ state before the forced context switch and reported that the reproducer worked. Participants later considered it narrower than the root-cause fix, but it was not falsified and is therefore not marked as a blind path.

solution.intent: Fix machine.disable_irq()/machine.enable_irq() to use a FreeRTOS-aware critical section so the kernel knows interrupts are masked and a yield after releasing the GIL cannot deadlock on RISC-V.
solution.concrete_example: Replace the from-ISR interrupt masking path with the appropriate FreeRTOS critical-section mechanism, preserving and restoring the prior IRQ state. Then ask the reporter to retest the original ESP32-C3 loop in a current build containing the change.
solution.inference_hint: The reporter supplied the reduced threshold, raw vPortYield/mp_thread_mutex_unlock stack, platform matrix, and first-bad revision. The maintainer inferred that MicroPython's from-ISR interrupt API hid the critical section from FreeRTOS, allowing the forced task yield after a GIL unlock to hang on the affected RISC-V ports.

edges.comment: Maintainer c28 gives the final accepted diagnosis and submits the candidate upstream fix. The visible thread contains no reporter result from testing that upstream build, so the terminal state records acceptance of the fix but does not claim reporter-verified resolution. The later memory-accounting discussion is unrelated and omitted.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the final root cause: MicroPython used a from-ISR interrupt-masking API for machine.disable_irq(), so FreeRTOS did not know it was in a critical section; the forced yield after releasing the GIL could then hang on the affected RISC-V ESP32 ports.
Diagnosis must be grounded in the approximately 32-operation threshold, the vPortYield/mp_thread_mutex_unlock backtrace, the first-bad revision, and the C3/C6 versus Xtensa platform results.
The proper fix must use FreeRTOS-aware critical-section handling while preserving and restoring the prior IRQ state; merely increasing or disabling the watchdog does not fix the hang.
Must not settle on passing the saved state to machine.enable_irq() as the solution, because the complete reproducer already does that and still hangs.
The reporter's patch that skips a forced switch while IRQ is disabled may be described as a working temporary workaround, but it must not replace the accepted root-cause fix.
Must ask the reporter to retest the original reproducer on a build containing the accepted fix before declaring the issue verified on the reporter's hardware.

persona_hint.experience_level: Technically capable embedded MicroPython user who can rebuild firmware, change ESP-IDF and watchdog configuration, bisect commits, reduce a reproducer, and write a temporary C-level patch, while openly describing their understanding of scheduler internals as limited.
persona_hint.communication_style: Detailed, persistent, and cooperative; supplies progressively smaller tests, exact revisions and configurations, explains the real-time application requirement, and asks conceptual follow-up questions.
